chapter: Tiny Bradshaw, Teddy Hill and Europe
title: Musicians who stayed in Europe, and the concentration camp
summary: Freedom from segregation in Europe led many to stay; Freddie Johnson and Valaida Snow were interned in the war, and a friend in the French army offered Procope a job on the Ile de France.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I remember Sam W ooding told me when he was over there he had his band there, 10 or 12 years earlier. He had been warned not to take his band to Paris, because that was the best way to lose your musicians. Once they got to Paris, they --
Well, there were a lot of musicians who liked the --

Yeah, who liked it so much, because you know, -- for a lot of reasons. You know, because there wasn't -- things weren't segregated over there like they were over here, and they got -- there was more freedom of action, freedom of playing, and you could -- so there were a whole lot of musicians who just stayed and lived over there and raised families and whatever. You know, which was good for them, I suppose. Freddie Johnson was one that -- the pianist who I worked with Sapiro's band, he went over there and lived, and
when the war broke out he was even in a concentration camp.
Yeah. When the Germans put him in a concentration camp.
Yeah, Valaida Snow was in a concentration camp.
Yeah. Yeah. And I know another fellow, Cooper -- what was his first name? He was living in France. He had a job at one time working on a -- what was the name of that French boat, a big French boat.
The Ile de France, in a band on the ship, and when the war started he was even in the French Army. Yeah. Yeah. And he came to -- he too offered me a job on the boat.
On the boat. Yeah. Of course I didn't take that either. Yeah.
